strengths: The approach addresses a useful problem: incorporating scene descriptions into affine-invariant depth estimation and allowing users to emphasize particular objects. Reusing Stable Diffusion’s text conditioning provides a simple, practically motivated extension of Marigold.

Evaluation covers four real-world datasets after depth training on synthetic data. At 30,000 iterations, PriorDiffusion improves both reported metrics over the reproduced Marigold baseline on every dataset; AbsRel decreases from 6.1 to 5.9 on NYUv2, 10.7 to 10.4 on KITTI, 6.9 to 6.5 on ETH3D, and 7.3 to 6.7 on ScanNet.

The small-region experiment provides quantitative support beyond whole-image averages: for NYUv2 masks occupying less than 5% of an image, δ1 improves from 91.7 to 92.8 and AbsRel decreases from 9.0 to 8.3. The qualitative examples illustrate a potentially useful interactive capability.

The supplement includes prompt variations, blank and generic-text comparisons, denoising-step sweeps, and substantial training details. These experiments support some benefit from scene-specific descriptions, while the incorrect-caption example candidly demonstrates a failure mode.
weaknesses: The principal contribution is adding scene-specific text through an existing conditioning pathway to a largely unchanged Marigold formulation. The stronger interpretation—that gains specifically demonstrate geometric knowledge recovered from text-to-image pretraining—is not isolated from additional information supplied by LLaVA or effects of caption-conditioned training. Table 5 shows that generic prompts retain much of the improvement. Controlled training ablations with generic or shuffled captions would materially strengthen the scientific attribution.

The efficiency claims exceed the measurements. Supplement B.2 reports 740 GPU-hours for training-caption generation, versus approximately 96 hours for depth-model training to convergence. Caption generation also costs approximately 3.6 seconds per test image. Fewer optimizer iterations and denoising steps are supported, but overall computational savings are not demonstrated without accounting for these costs and measuring end-to-end latency.

The broad state-of-the-art claim is not supported by Table 1: Depth Anything variants outperform PriorDiffusion on NYUv2, KITTI, and ScanNet, while GeoWizard also leads on several metrics. This does not negate the method’s value, but its demonstrated advantage is narrower. Gains over the published Marigold results are small on NYUv2 and KITTI, and no repeated-run variability is reported.

The evidence for controllable, region-specific improvement remains incomplete. Figure 6 presents one progressive-caption example without quantitative errors or a stated fixed-noise control. Table 2 evaluates all small segmentation regions rather than separating described from undescribed regions, so it does not establish that mentioning an object causes its improvement. Robustness to misleading descriptions is illustrated only qualitatively.

Several implementation and evaluation inconsistencies impede reproducibility. Section 3 specifies epsilon prediction, whereas Supplement B.2 specifies a v-objective; the displayed inference update does not describe the stated DDIM sampler. Supplement Eq. (3) aligns predictions against themselves rather than ground truth as written, and Eq. (2) reverses the normalization denominator relative to main-text Eq. (1). These may be correctable documentation errors, but the actual objective and evaluation procedure cannot be determined confidently from the manuscript.

The denoising comparison needs reconciliation with the main results: Supplement Table 4 reports Marigold’s 50-step KITTI performance as 88.5/11.2, versus 90.4/10.5 for published Marigold and 89.7/10.7 for the 30,000-iteration reproduction in Table 1. The checkpoint or configuration difference is not explained. Overall, the consistent practical gains place the paper near the acceptance boundary, but modest methodological novelty and unresolved evidence behind the central mechanism and efficiency claims prevent a stronger recommendation.

strengths: The method addresses a useful problem: incorporating scene descriptions into affine-invariant monocular depth estimation, including user-directed refinement of specific objects. Reusing Stable Diffusion’s text-conditioning pathway provides a simple, plausible implementation.

Evaluation covers four real-world datasets after depth training on synthetic data. At 30,000 iterations, Table 1 reports consistently lower AbsRel than the reproduced Marigold baseline: 5.9 versus 6.1 on NYUv2, 10.4 versus 10.7 on KITTI, 6.5 versus 6.9 on ETH3D, and 6.7 versus 7.3 on ScanNet. These improvements have value even without overall benchmark leadership.

Table 2 provides quantitative support for improved small-region prediction: for masks occupying less than 5% of an image, δ1 increases from 91.7 to 92.8 and AbsRel decreases from 9.0 to 8.3. The qualitative examples also suggest potentially useful sensitivity to object descriptions.

The supplementary material includes caption-generation prompts, training settings, alternative caption prompts, and blank/template-text controls. Figure 9 explicitly acknowledges that incorrect descriptions can damage predictions.
weaknesses: The central scientific attribution is insufficiently established. The method largely adds scene captions through the existing text-conditioning mechanism of a Marigold-style model. Table 5 supports the usefulness of informative captions, but it does not distinguish geometric knowledge inherited from text-to-image pretraining from semantic information supplied by LLaVA or generic conditioning effects. There are no matched shuffled-caption or object-name-only controls. Consequently, the evidence supports a useful conditioning effect more clearly than the claimed mechanism, leaving the methodological and scientific advance limited.

The efficiency claims omit a substantial component of the evaluated pipeline. Supplementary Section B.2 reports 740 GPU-hours to generate training captions, whereas depth-model convergence takes approximately four days on the same GPU type. Fewer optimization iterations therefore do not establish lower total training cost. At inference, caption generation takes approximately 3.6 seconds per image, but no end-to-end latency comparison includes this cost. The narrower claim of fewer denoising steps is supported; the broader computational-efficiency claim is not.

The inference-speed comparison has an unresolved baseline discrepancy. Table 4 reports Marigold’s 50-step AbsRel as 6.3/11.2/6.9/7.5 across the four datasets, differing from both the published and reproduced Marigold results in Table 1. The manuscript does not explain the checkpoint or configuration difference. This matters because the 10-versus-25-step convergence claim depends directly on the baseline used. No repeated-run uncertainty is provided to contextualize the relatively small headline accuracy gains.

The strong controllability claim exceeds its quantitative evidence. Figure 6 illustrates successive caption edits on one scene without numerical region-level errors or a stated fixed-noise protocol. Table 2 evaluates small masks generally, without establishing which masks are mentioned in captions or measuring the effect of adding and removing their descriptions. It demonstrates better small-region performance, but does not isolate reliable user-directed improvement. Robustness to inaccurate descriptions is illustrated only by a failure example.

Several technical inconsistencies impede reproducibility. Section 3 specifies noise prediction, while Supplementary B.2 states that training uses the v-objective. The displayed reverse update does not specify the DDIM procedure used experimentally. Supplementary Eq. (3) fits aligned predictions to the original predictions rather than ground truth, and Eq. (2) reverses the normalization denominator relative to main-text Eq. (1). These may be correctable exposition errors rather than implementation defects, but the submitted account does not unambiguously define the actual training and evaluation procedures.

The state-of-the-art claims are overstated: Table 1 shows substantially better NYUv2, KITTI, and ScanNet results for Depth Anything variants, and several relevant diffusion methods discussed in Related Work are absent from the quantitative comparison. Benchmark leadership is not required for acceptance, but the supported contribution is a modest improvement over Marigold with added language supervision. Taken together with the unresolved mechanism and efficiency claims, the current evidence favors weak rejection.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, useful extension of diffusion-based depth estimation: conditioning a Marigold-style model on image descriptions through the pretrained text-conditioning pathway. Language-guided refinement of objects of interest is a relevant capability beyond aggregate benchmark performance.

Evaluation covers four real-world datasets after depth training on synthetic data. At 30,000 iterations, Table 1 reports consistently lower AbsRel than the reimplemented Marigold: 6.1 to 5.9 on NYUv2, 10.7 to 10.4 on KITTI, 6.9 to 6.5 on ETH3D, and 7.3 to 6.7 on ScanNet. The matched training-data comparison and evaluation without ensembling are valuable.

The small-region evaluation provides quantitative support beyond selected visualizations. For NYUv2 regions occupying less than 5% of an image, Table 2 improves delta1 from 91.7 to 92.8 and AbsRel from 9.0 to 8.3.

The supplementary experiments examine caption-generation prompts, generic text inputs, and denoising-step counts. Table 5 supports an advantage from scene-specific descriptions over blank or generic inputs, while Figure 9 candidly illustrates vulnerability to incorrect descriptions.

The manuscript supplies substantial implementation information, including caption-generation prompts, data splits, optimization settings, and caption-generation costs. The training curves and denoising-step sweep support faster convergence in iteration and sampling-step counts.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is not sufficiently isolated. The architecture largely retains existing latent diffusion machinery and activates its text-conditioning pathway. Inference-time blank/template ablations do not establish whether gains specifically reflect geometric knowledge from text-to-image pretraining, additional knowledge supplied by LLaVA, or general conditioning effects. Matched training controls with fixed or shuffled captions are absent. The broad novelty claim also needs sharper differentiation from cited language-conditioned perception work such as VPD and WorDepth.

The efficiency conclusion exceeds the demonstrated evidence. Supplement B.2 reports 740 GPU-hours for training-caption generation, compared with approximately four days for depth-model convergence, and 3.6 seconds to generate each test caption. Fewer depth-training iterations and denoising steps therefore do not establish lower total computational cost or end-to-end latency. No complete timing comparison is provided.

The evidence for controllable, object-specific improvement remains limited. Table 2 evaluates small segmentation regions without establishing which are mentioned in captions, so it does not directly measure the claimed causal benefit of describing a particular object. Figure 6 is illustrative, but lacks quantitative regional errors and a stated fixed-noise comparison. Robustness to missing, contradictory, or hallucinated descriptions is represented by only a qualitative failure example.

The state-of-the-art claim is overstated by Table 1: Depth Anything variants substantially outperform PriorDiffusion on NYUv2, KITTI, and ScanNet, while GeoWizard is also stronger on some datasets. Different training budgets make the matched Marigold comparison more informative, but that comparison shows modest gains without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Moreover, the Marigold results in the supplementary denoising-step table differ from both Table 1 baselines without a clear explanation of the checkpoint or configuration.

Several technical inconsistencies hinder reproducibility. Section 3 specifies epsilon prediction, whereas Supplement B.2 states that training uses the v-objective. The presented reverse update does not specify the implemented subsampled DDIM procedure. Supplement Eq. (3) fits aligned predictions to the unaligned prediction rather than ground truth as written, and its normalization denominator reverses the sign used in main-text Eq. (1). These may be correctable documentation errors, but the manuscript does not unambiguously define the actual implementation.

Overall, the consistent cross-dataset improvements and promising language interaction place the paper near the acceptance boundary. However, the limited separation of the proposed mechanism from existing conditioning machinery, incomplete evidence for controllability, and unsupported end-to-end efficiency claims prevent a clear acceptance recommendation.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, useful way to condition diffusion-based depth estimation on scene descriptions through the pretrained text interface. Its potential value includes human-guided depth correction, even without achieving the best benchmark performance.

Table 1 provides reasonably broad evidence: three estimator families, including both Lotus variants, are evaluated on five real-world datasets after synthetic-data training. Text at training and inference improves nearly all metrics against the corresponding retrained baselines. For example, Marigold's ScanNet AbsRel decreases from 7.3% to 6.7%, and Lotus-D's KITTI δ1 increases from 92.2% to 93.0%.

The small-region evaluation supports a specific benefit beyond aggregate accuracy. In Table 2, NYUv2 regions occupying less than 5% of the image improve from 91.7% to 92.8% δ1, compared with a 0.2-point improvement overall. Qualitative examples illustrate plausible improvements on small and partially obscured objects.

The training-only/inference-only comparisons, caption-generation prompt ablations, caption-count experiments, and denoising-step sweep provide useful characterization. The paper also explicitly demonstrates that incorrect descriptions can harm predictions.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited to supplying captions through an existing conditioning mechanism; the main contribution is therefore empirical. The stronger explanation—that pretrained text-conditioned 3D knowledge specifically resolves depth ambiguity—is not isolated experimentally. Generated captions also introduce knowledge from a substantial external vision-language model. Generic-prompt experiments help, but there is no matched shuffled-caption or semantic-content control separating scene-specific geometric information from general conditioning effects.

Baseline reliability limits confidence in the magnitude of the gains. Several retrained baselines substantially underperform the cited results: E2E-FT's NYUv2 AbsRel is 6.9% versus 5.4%, and Lotus-G's ETH3D AbsRel is 9.2% versus 5.9%. The paper acknowledges unreproduced results, and comparisons against matched retraining remain informative, but does not explain these gaps sufficiently. Many improvements are small and lack repeated-run variability or confidence intervals.

The efficiency evidence establishes fewer denoising steps, not end-to-end speedup. Appendix B.2 reports approximately 3.6 seconds per generated caption and 740 GPU-hours for Marigold's training captions, yet no total latency or training-cost comparison incorporates these costs. The benefit is more credible when descriptions are already available; faster diffusion convergence alone does not establish overall computational efficiency.

The interactive-refinement claim is supported primarily by one qualitative sequence in Figure 6, without ground-truth error measurements, repeated examples, or controls for sampling randomness. Similarly, Table 2 evaluates all small segmentation regions rather than separating objects explicitly mentioned in captions. These experiments support local improvements but do not firmly establish reliable, targeted refinement through additional language.

Reproducibility has substantive inconsistencies. The main text specifies one caption per image, whereas Appendix B.2 describes ten for Marigold. Table 4's 50-step Marigold baseline differs from Table 1 without a clear configuration explanation. Appendix B.3's alignment objective compares aligned predictions with unaligned predictions rather than ground truth, and its metric equations do not consistently use aligned depth. These appear potentially correctable, but the provided manuscript leaves the actual evaluation protocol ambiguous.

Overall, the breadth and consistency of the matched comparisons make this a worthwhile empirical contribution. However, limited methodological novelty, uncertainty around baseline reproduction, and incomplete support for the efficiency and interactive-refinement claims keep the recommendation at the decision boundary.

strengths: The paper studies a useful, practical question: whether restoring text conditioning in pretrained diffusion models improves monocular depth estimation. The integration is simple and applicable to multiple existing estimators.

Table 1 provides reasonably broad evidence across Marigold, Lotus-D, Lotus-G, and E2E-FT on five real-world datasets after synthetic-data training. Joint training and inference conditioning improves almost every reported metric relative to the corresponding retrained baseline. For example, Marigold’s ScanNet AbsRel decreases from 7.3% to 6.7%, and its DIODE δ1 increases from 77.0% to 78.9%.

The small-region evaluation adds evidence beyond aggregate accuracy: for NYUv2 masks occupying less than 5% of an image, δ1 increases from 91.7% to 92.8% and AbsRel decreases from 9.0% to 8.3%. Qualitative examples illustrate plausible benefits for otherwise overlooked objects.

The supplementary experiments examine caption prompts, caption counts, fixed inference prompts, and denoising steps. The paper also explicitly demonstrates a failure caused by incorrect text, acknowledging a meaningful limitation.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the approach supplies captions through the pretrained model’s existing text-conditioning pathway, with no substantial new architecture or objective. Its contribution therefore depends primarily on the empirical findings, but the proposed explanation—recovering geometric conditions learned during text-to-image pretraining—is not isolated experimentally. There are no shuffled-caption or matched generic-caption training controls to distinguish scene-specific geometric information from broader conditioning or regularization effects.

The reliability and practical magnitude of improvements remain uncertain. Several gains are small, with no repeated-run variability reported, while some reproduced baselines fall substantially below the published results. For example, Lotus-G’s ETH3D AbsRel is 9.2% when reproduced versus 5.9% reported originally, and text only reduces it to 9.0%. Matched retraining comparisons remain useful, but unexplained reproduction gaps limit conclusions about improvements to well-performing implementations.

Two central claims receive weaker support than the aggregate accuracy claim. Iterative refinement is demonstrated through one qualitative example in Figure 6, without quantitative evaluation or a stated fixed-noise control. Table 2 evaluates small segmentation regions generally, without separating caption-mentioned regions from unmentioned regions, so it does not establish that explicit textual mentions cause the localized improvements.

The efficiency claim concerns iteration and denoising-step counts rather than end-to-end cost. The supplement reports approximately 3.6 seconds per generated caption and 740 GPU-hours for its ten-caption training collection, but provides no combined caption-generation and depth-inference timings. The reduced-step results are promising, especially when text is already available, but do not establish an overall computational saving for the evaluated automatic-caption pipeline.

Technical reporting contains consequential ambiguities. Section 3 describes epsilon prediction and a reverse update that does not specify the DDIM implementation, whereas the supplement reports v-prediction and DDIM sampling for Marigold and E2E-FT. The main text specifies one caption per image, while the Marigold implementation describes generating ten; the connection between these configurations and individual tables is insufficiently explicit. Supplementary Table 4 also reports different 50-step baseline results from Table 1 without clearly explaining the configuration change.

Overall, the consistent cross-model improvements and small-region results constitute a worthwhile empirical contribution. However, limited novelty, unresolved experimental comparability, and insufficient support for the stronger mechanism, refinement, and efficiency claims keep the manuscript near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The paper provides a useful empirical contribution: restoring language conditioning in pretrained diffusion depth estimators generally improves relative-depth prediction. The consistent results across three model families and five real-world datasets support weak acceptance, despite limited architectural novelty.

Table 1 includes retrained baselines and separates training-only, inference-only, and joint text conditioning. Joint conditioning improves both metrics across all five datasets for Marigold, Lotus-D, and Lotus-G. For example, Marigold’s ScanNet AbsRel decreases from 7.3% to 6.7%, and its DIODE δ1 increases from 77.0% to 78.9%.

The small-region evaluation supports a practically relevant benefit beyond aggregate benchmark gains. On NYUv2 masks occupying less than 5% of the image, δ1 increases from 91.7% to 92.8% and AbsRel decreases from 9.0% to 8.3%, exceeding the corresponding whole-image improvements.

The supplementary experiments investigate caption-generation prompts, caption counts, fixed inference prompts, and denoising steps. Table 4 provides evidence that text-conditioned Marigold reaches strong accuracy with fewer denoising steps.

The approach is simple and compatible with existing pretrained components. Qualitative examples illustrate potential language-guided depth correction, and Figure 9 candidly demonstrates a failure caused by incorrect text.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is primarily empirical: the method supplies captions through an existing text-conditioning pathway while retaining established diffusion training machinery. The explanation that pretrained language conditioning reduces geometric ambiguity is plausible but not isolated experimentally. Shuffled-caption controls, controlled spatial-description edits, or comparisons against conditioning without pretrained text associations would better distinguish scene-specific guidance from general conditioning effects.

Several gains are small, and no repeated-run variability or uncertainty estimates are reported. Retrained baselines also substantially underperform published results in some cases: Lotus-G’s ETH3D AbsRel is 9.2% versus 5.9% reported, and adding text only reduces it to 9.0%. These gaps do not invalidate the matched comparisons, but they limit confidence that the improvements transfer to fully reproduced baseline performance.

The efficiency evidence establishes fewer iterations or denoising steps, rather than lower end-to-end cost. The supplement reports approximately 3.6 seconds per generated caption and 740 GPU-hours for the ten-caption training collection. Without wall-clock comparisons including caption generation and text encoding, the broader efficiency claim remains conditional on descriptions already being available.

Language-guided iterative refinement is illustrated by a selected example rather than evaluated systematically. The small-region experiment groups masks by size without establishing whether each region is mentioned in the caption. Consequently, improved small-region accuracy is supported more strongly than reliable correction of specifically described objects. Robustness to incomplete or inaccurate captions is likewise only demonstrated qualitatively.

Reproducibility is weakened by inconsistent descriptions. The main text specifies one caption per image, whereas the Marigold implementation section describes ten; the main formulation predicts noise, while implementation details specify a v-objective. Supplementary Eq. (2) fits aligned predictions to the original prediction rather than ground truth as written, and the normalization equation has a reversed percentile denominator. These appear correctable documentation errors, but the actual configurations and evaluation implementation need clarification.
